chunks: In critical applications such as medical imaging and diagnostic systems, well-calibrated models are paramount for ensuring accurate and trustworthy outcomes. By aligning predicted probabilities with the true likelihood of events, well-calibrated predictors reduce the discrepancy between a model's confidence and actual results, fostering user trust and minimizing the need for post-processing calibration methods (e.g., temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017) or isotonic regression (Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana, 2005)). However, while Focal Loss (Lin et al., 2017) effectively addresses class imbalance, it often leads to overly confident predictions (Charoenphakdee et al., 2021). This shortfall highlights the post-processing gap-the difference between raw model outputs and the properly calibrated probabilities required for reliable decision-making. Recent studies have further established focal loss's theoretical foundation in classification calibration (Charoenphakdee et al., 2021), showing that a classifier trained with focal loss can achieve the optimal Bayes classifier in theory. Nevertheless, focal loss is not a proper scoring rule, and training with it can yield underconfident or overconfident estimators-unreliable for class-posterior probability estimation.

Recent studies have further established focal loss's theoretical foundation in classification calibration (Charoenphakdee et al., 2021), showing that a classifier trained with focal loss can achieve the optimal Bayes classifier in theory. Nevertheless, focal loss is not a proper scoring rule, and training with it can yield underconfident or overconfident estimators-unreliable for class-posterior probability estimation. Proper scoring rules, such as the Brier score (Brier, 1950) or log-loss, encourage models to produce unbiased class-posterior probabilities (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017) and ensure that postprocessing does not significantly reduce the loss (Blasiok et al., 2024). Building on these insights, our work investigates whether integrating a proper loss into focal loss can improve its calibration as a class-posterior probability estimator. Our key contributions are:

• Focal Calibration Loss (FCL): We propose a new loss function that combines the traditional Focal Loss with a proper calibration term, uniquely aligning predicted probabilities with true class-posterior probabilities to mitigate overconfidence and underconfidence. • Theoretical Guarantees: We prove that minimizing FCL yields superior probability and classification calibration compared to Focal Loss alone, effectively reducing the post-processing gap.

Improving the calibration of deep neural networks (DNNs) is critical for reliable uncertainty estimation. A common strategy involves post-hoc calibration methods, which adjust a pre-trained model's output probabilities without altering its architecture or training procedure. Platt scaling (Platt et al., 1999), originally designed for binary classifiers, was extended to multi-class settings by applying a linear transformation to logits to improve calibration. More recent methods like Temperature Scaling (Guo et al., 2017) introduce a temperature parameter to adjust the predicted logits, effectively reducing the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) across various models. Histogram Binning (Zadrozny & Elkan, 2002) discretizes the probability space into bins to align confidence scores with empirical frequencies. While effective, these methods require held-out validation data and assume the test distribution matches the calibration data. Regularization Calibration for transformer-based architectures, now prevalent in both vision and language domains, is increasingly essential for reliable deployment in high-stakes applications.

Regularization Calibration for transformer-based architectures, now prevalent in both vision and language domains, is increasingly essential for reliable deployment in high-stakes applications. In NLP, foundational transformer models such as BERT (Devlin, 2018), GPT (Brown, 2020), and T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) often lead the field in accuracy yet suffer from miscalibrated confidence (Desai & Durrett, 2020;Jiang et al., 2020), especially under out-of-distribution conditions (Mielke et al., 2022). Likewise, vision transformers (ViTs) exhibit calibration issues under distribution shifts (Ovadia et al., 2019), adversarial attacks (Shao et al., 2021), and low-data scenarios (Minderer et al., 2021). These limitations underscore the need for robust calibration methods to enhance reliability in domains such as autonomous driving (Feng et al., 2021) and medical imaging (Mehrtash et al., 2020). In conclusion, traditional Focal Loss has been instrumental in reducing misclassification rates by focusing on hardto-classify samples; however, it often falls short in providing well-calibrated predictions. By ensuring that the loss function is strictly proper, FCL delivers more reliable class-posterior probabilities, which directly contributes to improved model confidence and reliability across various applications even in unforeseen circumstances.

By ensuring that the loss function is strictly proper, FCL delivers more reliable class-posterior probabilities, which directly contributes to improved model confidence and reliability across various applications even in unforeseen circumstances. Ensuring accurate and trustworthy confidence scores in deep neural networks is vital for deploying them in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and finance. By introducing a focal calibration loss that leverages an explicit Euclidean distance term, our approach not only addresses class imbalance but also reduces miscalibration, aligning model outputs with real-world outcome frequencies. This dual improvement in accuracy and reliability fosters greater transparency and confidence when models are used to assist critical decisions.
